title: Financial Dashboard & Payment Automation
short: Making complex payments easier to manage.
summary: Connecting financial data, recurring subscriptions and exception handling in one Laravel application.
problem: A customer can have several subscriptions, different payment intervals and changing prices. A customer ID alone does not tell you which payment belongs to which subscription or period. Late payments and reversals make that matching more difficult.
role: I developed the internal application at Xeropex, translating the owner's business requirements into backend logic and financial views. I worked independently on the implementation within the company's development and review process.
approach: I retrieved the base financial records through the Exact Online API and handled filtering, calculations and business rules in the Laravel application. Matching logic considered the customer, active recurring payments, expected dates, intervals and prices, including possible price changes. Filament provided the dashboard views.
challenge: The difficult part was distinguishing a changed subscription from a new, unrelated recurring payment. I had to consider several pieces of information together, rather than treating a matching price or customer as sufficient. Keeping application-side processing separate from data retrieval also helped work within Exact Online's API-call limits.
result: The application brought income, expenses, subscriptions and payment statuses into a shared dashboard. I added status monitoring and email notifications for arrears and exceptions so records needing attention could be followed up.
evidence: The implementation belongs to Xeropex and its source code is private. The illustration below explains the workflow using fictional records; it is not a screenshot of the internal application.

title: Local AI Chat & Business Reporting
short: From a question to a useful business report.
summary: A local Ollama model connected to explicit Laravel functions through structured command processing.
problem: Business questions often require several steps: select a period, retrieve the relevant records, calculate results and present them clearly. A chat model alone cannot perform those application-specific operations or access an isolated database.
role: I built the chat interface and the backend connection between the locally running model and the application's data and reporting functions at Xeropex.
approach: I used prompts to ask the model for a structured text command. My own PHP/Laravel code extracted that command with regex and checks, then used programmed application functions to retrieve data and calculate results. The response could include report text, tables and charts. The model itself did not have direct database access.
challenge: A language-model response cannot simply be treated as an application instruction. The integration needed to recognise the expected format and check the requested values before processing them. Different prompts and application functions handled different parts of the workflow; this was not model training or an autonomous agent system.
result: The application connected natural-language questions to business reporting through backend functions. The central contribution was the integration: translating model output into data processing and a readable answer.
evidence: The business application and source code are private. The chat shown here is an explanatory illustration with fictional figures, not a live AI service or a production screenshot.

title: AI Website Analysis & Prototype Generation
short: Turning website research into a tangible prototype.
summary: A pipeline for extracting website content, comparing features and generating multi-page website prototypes.
problem: Showing a prospective customer a proposed website can require considerable work before there is an agreement. Xeropex wanted a way to explore possible improvements and produce a testable visual starting point.
role: I developed the workflow for collecting website information, comparing it with a configurable feature list and connecting that context to AI-generated website files.
approach: The pipeline used website input and extracted content to inventory existing features and identify gaps against a desired feature list. I worked on the prompts and file processing needed to generate a prototype with multiple pages. I also explored batch processing as a trade-off between cost and completion time.
challenge: Generating the appearance of a feature is different from implementing its backend behaviour. Multi-page output also needs consistent navigation and shared assets. The generated result should therefore be reviewed as a prototype, with simulated interactions identified before further development.
result: A downloadable example from the original portfolio contains 28 HTML pages and accompanying assets. It demonstrates multi-page generation and gives a concrete starting point for discussing a website redesign.
evidence: The original portfolio states that Xeropex allowed this generated example to be shared. Download and extract the ZIP, then open index.html. Some interactions are simulated; the example has no production backend.

title: Commercial Web Application Maintenance
summary: Bug fixes, customer requests and new features in established Laravel codebases at Xeropex.
problem: Existing customer applications need maintenance as well as new features. Changes must fit the surrounding code and avoid disrupting existing behaviour.
role: During internships and paid development work at Xeropex, I handled tickets, investigated bugs and implemented customer requests in existing applications.
approach: I worked with Git branches, debugging, unit tests and code reviews before changes were merged and released. Understanding the existing code was part of the work, rather than replacing it with a new implementation.
challenge: In one case, a price filter could enter an infinite loop under certain conditions and freeze the browser. I worked on a fix that placed boundaries on the input or processing. The lesson was to check edge cases and termination conditions, not only the expected input.
result: This work gave me practical experience maintaining shared code, responding to feedback and contributing changes within a development team.
evidence: Customer code remains private. This case describes my responsibilities and a debugging example without publishing confidential implementation details.

title: Personal Developer Portfolio
short: A static home for my development work.
summary: From an earlier Laravel and Blade portfolio to a static site that works on GitHub Pages.
problem: The portfolio needs to make my experience understandable quickly and give each project a direct, shareable link. It also needs to work without a PHP server.
role: My earlier portfolio used Laravel and Blade. This redesigned static edition was created with AI assistance; it presents my projects and preserves their existing URLs.
approach: The current site uses semantic HTML, shared CSS and a small JavaScript enhancement for project filters and mobile navigation. A Python build script renders pages from central project content. The published output needs no server, runtime dependencies or build service.
challenge: GitHub Pages can serve the site under a repository subdirectory. Relative asset and page links avoid depending on the domain root. Project text and navigation are rendered into the HTML, so the primary content remains available without JavaScript.
result: A responsive portfolio with direct case-study URLs, an up-to-date software CV, accessible navigation and email contact. It makes professional software work the main entry point, with game projects available separately.
evidence: The original public repository documents the earlier versions. This redesign should be attributed separately from my original work; it is not evidence that I independently authored every part of this new design.

title: Winter Wonder Ride
short: Vehicle control, camera behaviour and power-ups.
summary: A Unity team project, also represented in the public NightRacer repository.
role: I worked on vehicle driving and steering with wheel colliders, a speedometer, camera-follow behaviour and power-ups. The team included other developers and artists.
approach: The camera followed the car and adjusted around walls. Vehicle movement included limits on rotation and handling for landing after airborne movement. Power-ups added speed and shield behaviour.
result: This project helped me work with interacting gameplay systems and shared responsibilities in a team.

title: Procedural Animation
summary: A personal Unity experiment using raycasts, interpolation and movement logic.
role: I explored procedural walking in my free time and wrote movement logic for a humanoid character.
approach: The implementation combined ground detection using raycasts with interpolated foot positions and step height. It was an opportunity to understand how individual calculations produce visible motion.
result: The experiment produced a procedural walking demonstration and gave me practice reasoning about movement over time.

title: Hack
summary: A Unity team game with two developers and three artists.
role: My contributions included enemy field of view, movement and states, power-ups and elevator animation.
approach: I worked on the connection between what an enemy can see and how it behaves, alongside player interactions and animation. These systems were parts of a larger team-made game.
result: The project gave me experience implementing several gameplay features while collaborating with developers and artists.

title: The Play
short: Attack logic and timed gameplay behaviour.
summary: A Unity project with programming by me and art from the asset store.
role: I programmed the game, including attack selection and coroutine-based behaviour. The artwork came from the asset store.
approach: I worked on the attack manager and on handling attempts to activate an attack that was already running. The chosen approach selected a different attack instead of simply cancelling the action.
result: The project gave me practice managing simultaneous actions and game state in C#.

title: The Rift Guardian
short: Blueprint contributions to a larger VR team game.
summary: An Unreal Engine VR project created by a larger development and art team.
role: I contributed Blueprint behaviour for a moon ability, including an explosion and shockwave. I did not create the moon model or texture, and the full game was a team effort.
approach: My work covered effects that grew and faded over time, as well as ability behaviour affecting nearby enemies and the player's health.
result: This was experience contributing a bounded feature to a much larger VR project and working within an existing team structure.
